speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to give my wholehearted support to the spirit behind this bill. I represent a constituency that suffers severe damage because of the failure of the C.P.R. to recognize its responsibility so far as passenger services are concerned.
[Mr. Southam.l
There are over 100,000 people in the south eastern section of B.C., and here we have a railway line running from Hope to Lethbridge, over which there is no passenger service as a result of the application of the C.P.R. being granted by the board of transport commissioners. Here we have air service which, during the winter months, can be intermittent on account of the weather which prevents aircraft landing at Castlegar airport, sometimes days at a time. Here we have road conditions where, owing to our usual snowfall, it is very difficult to keep communications open and to provide satisfactory transport facilities on the roads under certain circumstances.
This is a set of circumstances which means that a large number of persons in the southeastern interior of B.C. are not able to travel by plane, have not the opportunity to travel by train, and on occasion because of weather conditions are denied the opportunity to travel by road. This is a particularly serious matter when it comes to moving persons to the coast, persons who require medical treatment and things of that sort.
I am sure members of the house have heard my views on this question over and over again throughout the years, but owing to the fact that the C.P.R. refuses to accept its responsibility to the some 100,000 people I am speaking of, we now have no passenger service on what is generally known as the Kettle valley railway.
In my opinion the spirit of this bill is excellent. The hon. member has mentioned that on occasion the railway companies make applications for abandonment of rail lines. Possibly at the time they are refused, but they re-apply within a short time. This bill intends to make it certain that they must not re-apply before a certain period of time has elapsed.
Quite recently the C.P.R. decided to withdraw the station agent from the city of Ross-land, a city of 4,000 people, and said all the services could be performed from the city of Trail. It said that telegrams and other things could all be rerouted through Trail and sent from that point, whether they were out-going or in-coming. Now we are suffering the latest indignity. The C.P.R. has made application to the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. I shall now read a letter written by C. W. Rump, secretary of the board of transport commissioners, dated August 26, 1964:

Dear Sir:
File No. 39309.64-Application of the C.P.R. to abandon part of its Rossland subdivision from Warfield (mile 21.8) to Rossland, B.C. (mile 29.3) a distance of 7.5 miles.
In a letter dated August 7, 1964, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has made application as above noted.
For your information, the railway has forwarded a copy of this application to Mr. H. S. Elmes, mayor, 2115 Queen street, Rossland, B.C.; Mr. C. Waldman, president, chamber of commerce, 1502 First street, Rossland, B.C.; Mr. J. W. Channon, adviser to the minister on branch line rationalization, Canadian Department of Agriculture, Ottawa, and Mr. J. Murray, clerk-treasurer, village of Warfield, B.C. and the board has given them until October 7, 1964 to file any representations they may care to make in this matter.
Yours very truly,
C. W. Rump,
Secretary.
In writing that letter Mr. Rump was only performing his duty as secretary of the board of transport commissioners. I received the letter toward the end of August, and later I received a letter from W. H. Vickers, city clerk of Rossland, B.C., in which he said: Dear sir:
Re: C.P.R. application for abandonment of rail service Warfield to Rossland.
Sorry for the delay in answering your letter of September 18 with regard to the above subject.
After considerable study city council arrived at the decision that they would not object to the removal of the majority of track within the city limits providing rail service is maintained from Warfield to the vicinity of the Rossland southerly boundary.
It is felt that in view of the renewed mining activity in this immediate area and in view of the fact that coal, flour and feed and a certain amount of oil and heavy equipment are supplied by rail the rail service should not be terminated to this city. There is 1.78 miles of mainline and 1.21 miles of sidings within the city boundaries. Council would consent to this removal.
Please advise if there is any other information you require.
As a result of the opposition of the city council, the chamber of commerce and other organizations, it was arranged that an inspector would go to Rossland to hear representations. I received another letter from C. W. Rump, secretary of the board of transport commissioners, dated November 27, 1964, in which he said:
Dear Sir:
Further to your letter dated August 10, 1964, please be advised that the board's district inspector at Saskatoon will review this matter on the ground, arriving in that area on December 1, 1964.
For your information, the municipal authorities have been advised by the inspector as to his visit for that purpose.
Railway Act
This inspector went to Rossland and representations were made on behalf of the city of Rossland which, as I have previously informed the house, is a city of 4,000 people, on behalf of the chamber of commerce, on behalf of other organizations and other persons, protesting most vigorously against the abandonment of this section of the Rossland subdivision, and rightly so. The city council, the chamber of commerce and other organizations presented very good evidence to prove that the removal of this section of the subdivision would cause a hardship to the city of Rossland.
This city is one of the highest in Canada. Large quantities of coal are moved into it for fuel every winter, large quantities of oil, and of course flour, groceries and other commodities, the basic requirements necessary for a city of 4,000 people; and now the C.P.R., having first done away with the station agent, is asking to abandon this section of the Rossland subdivision. You can imagine the protest there was against this. I received telegrams and letters from various persons and organizations.
The inspector heard the arguments, which I think were sound and valid on the basis of the circumstances that exist, and I understand he made a report to the board of transport commissioners. I also understand that the Canadian Pacific Railway has the opportunity of going over the evidence collected by the inspector in order to prepare its argument against the argument presented by the representatives of the people who are going to be affected.
I further understand that the city of Rossland and the chamber of commerce would like to know what are the arguments of the Canadian Pacific Railway against those presented by the organizations in Rossland.
In addition, I have received from the city clerk a letter dated February 10 which reads as follows:
Mr. C. W. Rump, Secretary Board of Transport Commissioners,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
I have been instructed by City Council to advise you that the City of Rossland herewith endorses the brief dated December 8, 1964 submitted to you by the Rossland Chamber of Commerce in protest against the abandonment of rail services between Warfield and Rossland.
Yours truly,
W. H. Vickers,
City Clerk.

Railway Act
This letter endorses wholeheartedly the brief prepared by the chamber of commerce after a thorough survey of the need of the city of Rossland for this type of transportation. The question is still under consideration. I have received further correspondence with regard to it and I have been informed that as a result of the continued interest taken in this subject and of the concern felt by the people I have the honour to represent, the board of transport commissioners-
The member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) laughs when I say "I have the honour to represent". I am honoured to have represented the people of Kootenay West for 20 years and I do not back down before anybody in that respect.

Fortunately the board of
transport commissioners has agreed that as the result of the great interest in this question and the concern of the residents of Rossland over the abandonment of this service, hearings are to be held in the area. At the present time various organizations in the city are preparing briefs and arguments to present to the board when it visits the area to hear the case against the abandonment of this line.
In the first instance I referred to the unfortunate lack of a sense of responsibility on the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway with respect to passenger service between Vancouver and Lethbridge. I am dealing now with lack of responsibility to the people of Canada by this attempt to abandon this section of the Rossland subdivision. It is because of these repeated experiences in my own constituency and in the constituency of the hon. member for Kootenay East, which is affected as far as the denial of passenger service is concerned just as much as we are in Kootenay West and in the south Okanagan, that I rise to express my complete support for the principle and purpose of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk). I am sure it has been introduced as a result of his experience and as a result of the experience of his constituents with the same type of attitude on the part of the C.P.R.
That is all I have to say at this time because I know there are others who are anxious to take part in this debate and carry on. I see the hon. member for Medicine Hat leaning forward ready to rise and support our arguments, and realizing this, I give the floor to

him willingly and hope he will keep going till six o'clock.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPEATED APPLICATIONS FOR ABANDONMENT
speechtext:
I hate to rob the hon. member for Medicine Hat of his opportunity to present arguments in favour of the bill, but I should like to get on the record a few arguments from the other side of the fence. I am opposed to this particular bill.
I admit that I live in eastern Canada where rail line abandonment is not the same problem as it is in the west. We think about it differently. One of the statements made in the MacPherson report struck me as being significant. The commission said there were some 8,600 miles of uneconomic railway line scattered across Canada. I tend to look at this situation from the point of view that these lines have to be paid for and that they can only be paid for either by shippers who have to bear the cost in the form of increased freight rates, or by subsidies out of public funds, resulting in increased taxation. This causes concern in the manufacturing areas of the east because anything which adds to the cost of shipping our goods tends to make us less competitive in the markets we seek outside this country. So, looking at a situation of this kind, our natural inclination is to ask: Is there any way in which we can get rid of these uneconomic factors.
I realize that in taking this attitude we must not ignore the other side of the argument. We must realize that the local public interest in the areas directly concerned should also be borne in mind and that the needs of the communities served by these lines have to be taken into consideration. The present practice is for the board of transport commissioners to try to resolve these countervailing points of view and arrive at the best possible decision in the public interest of the whole country, weighing the local needs of the community against the economic needs of the nation. The board considers the applications which are made by the railway companies and rules on them, either favourable to or against abandonment. This particular bill would prevent railway companies from returning with an application within a period of five years. The explanatory note states, in this respect-and I will quote it, if I may:
The reason for the suggested amendments is that very often a railway company whose request has been turned down will renew its application from time to time, at short intervals, in the hope that the opposition has abated or will not be so active and consequently that the board will reverse its previous decision notwithstanding the fact that the situation is unchanged since the day of the original

demand. The new application is more in the nature of an appeal, from a refusal, to the same board.
It is my information that, in fact, this does not really happen. This is one of my major objections to the bill before us. It is my understanding, having spoken to the assistant secretary to the board, that there have been very few applications within the last ten years which have been in the nature of reapplications, and that those which have been received were made after a period of a year and a half, or two years or so, when there had been some change in the situation affecting the line which made such re-applications worth considering.
I gather, also, that about a year ago the C.N.R. submitted 75 proposals for abandonment and that out of this number only two were re-applications. Of those two, one had been made two and a half years earlier and the other had been made three years earlier. In both cases changes had taken place in the factors which affected the board's original decision. I also understand that when the board turns down an application it often does so on the understanding that should certain factors vary or change substantially-traffic revenue, for example,-the railway company may bring its application back for consideration.
My objection then, to the bill is that it seeks to cure a problem which does not in fact exist. I am also much concerned, and this is my second point, with the danger of the rigidity which would be established if the suggested procedure came into effect. It is entirely possible that an application would be made for the abandonment of a line and that it would be turned down on the ground that the line was essential to a certain industry, shall we say, that was using it. If the industry that was the sole reason for the refusal of application went out of business or no longer needed that line, under this legislation the railway would still have to carry that line, which would then probably have no really useful purpose, for a period of five years. I believe this is unduly rigid and unduly restrictive, and I think it could work hardship that is not necessary, because again I come back to the point that I do not believe a problem in fact exists of repetitive reapplications.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, to summarize my points thus far, I do not think there is a problem, and to apply this legislation would only add to a system rigidities that are not really necessary. Also, another major reason 20220-763
Railway Act
for not passing this specific piece of legislation is the fact that there is, as we know, a proposed bill, the subject matter of which is before the standing committee, and which will undoubtedly come forward next session, which will make major changes in the procedures for abandonment. 1 think the procedures outlined in that bill adequately deal with this complex problem of abandonment, and I do not think we could reasonably expect to pass this piece of legislation, even if it were good legislation, in view of the impending bill being brought forward next session.
As I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, the estimate of the MacPherson commission was that there were some 8,600 miles of uneconomic rail lines in the country. As I have indicated, this places a burden on those who pay the freight bills and it places a burden on the taxpayers who have to finance or pay for the subsidies that are necessary to keep these lines on the ground. I think the bill to be introduced next session recognizes these problems and seeks to find a reasonable means of eliminating them, at the same time taking into account and being aware of the need to provide service to the local communities. Under the procedure that is proposed in that bill, the railways will make an application, once they themselves have decided that a line is uneconomic, for the abandonment of that line, and they will file that application. The first thing to happen then is that the board has to verify that there is in fact a loss on the line, so that the railways will not be able to present spurious figures in the hope that they can abandon a line that they do not want to keep in operation. The figures will be checked and verified. If there is no loss on the line, obviously the application is rejected out of hand. But if the line is truly uneconomic, there is a problem and it is up to the rationalization authority to then decide what to do about the problem. The authority, in looking at the problem, will decide whether or not the line should be abandoned right away, whether it should be abandoned within a period of five years or, in exceptional cases, they may decide that the line should be kept in operation for a period as long as 15 years.
In making their decision they will be taking into account a series of factors, which I will indicate briefly. I think these factors cover the problems inherent in the abandonment of a railway line. They have to take into account the alternative transportation

Railway Act
facilities available, or likely to be available, in the area. They have to take into account the period of time required for the purpose of adjusting the facilities of those organizations that are dependant on the line. They have to take into account the probable effect on other lines, or other carriers, of the abandonment of any line. They have to take into account the feasibility of maintaining the line, or any segment of it, as an operating line by changing the method of operation of the line. In other words, Mr. Speaker, they will not only look at the line from the point of view of abandoning it; they will look at it to see if it cannot be made economic and what should be done to make it economic. They will also be looking to the future transportation needs of the area served by the line.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that if a line is proved to be uneconomic, the authority having looked at all the factors I have just indicated, including the possibility of making it economic, when they reach a decision with respect to abandonment they have a pretty clear picture of the needs of the community and the problem of the railroads, and they will reach a decision that will probably be the best decision that can be arrived at on the facts at hand.
Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be most unlikely that railways would suddenly, having had a rejection of an application, come back and try and harass the transportation authority. They have not done this in the past, and I do not think they are likely to do so when this new legislation comes into effect.
So, Mr. Speaker, to conclude my remarks I would say again that I do not think there is a problem now. I believe the proposed bill now before us is unduly restrictive and that the new legislation, that hopefully might be passed next session, will adequately deal with the problem of the abandonment of branch lines. I therefore would reject the passing of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the concern that the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) has with respect to this matter of railway line abandonment, but I am not sure that I agree with the method he advances in Bill No. C-79 to deal with that concern and problem. In the first place, when this bill was put on the order paper back on March 20, 1964, I think there was every justification for this kind of private member's public bill to be brought to the attention of this house, be-

cause this was before Bill No. C-120 or even the resolution preceding that bill was brought before the house. Certainly there is a great deal of concern, particularly on the prairies, as to what government policy is going to be and what will be the actions of the board of transport commissioners with respect to, first of all, the applications that are before it now for railway abandonment, and what they are going to do about anticipated applications for abandonment.
So far as I am concerned-and I think this is the policy of our party-we cannot take an absolutely rigid position that there shall be no railway abandonment at all, in spite of the economic factors that may be involved in any particular line. I know, for example, that there are railway lines in western Canada now which do not haul the mail; they do not have any passenger service; they do not haul any local freight-and in fact they are hauling very little grain. We have to be realistic about this matter, as the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hahn) mentioned, and if these lines are not being used we should not pay even the minimum costs necessary to keep them there or the costs specifically attributable to keeping them there. Then we have to be realistic and reasonable in giving some consideration to the fact that other means of transportation have taken over the uses and purposes for which that railway was laid down in the first place.
But one of the problems up to this time with respect to railway line abandonment is that there has been no policy. There was no policy set down by the previous government. So far there has been no policy from this government except the introduction of Bill No. C-120. If it is said that passage of Bill No. C-120 is going to completely solve this problem with regard to having a policy, I am not prepared to support that argument. I think we need to have as a national railway policy, or as part of a national railway policy, some kind of agreement on what is a minimum grid system of railways throughout the country. So far these railway abandonment applications have come in on a piecemeal basis. This cannot continue, because we may find ourselves in the situation where some of the railways which were in existence and which could be fitted into what would be a reasonable and realistic grid system will have been abandoned.
I think it is fair to say that the board of transport commissioners really have not moved very fast on granting railway abandonment applications. In fact I think there is almost a moratorium on them now. Therefore

I am not particularly concerned that there will be any wholesale abandonment until the provisions of Bill No. C-120 come into effect. I hope consideration will be given to the people who are going to suffer substantial financial losses as the result of railway line abandonment, and all these other communications disruptions which will take place. I hope that the board which is envisaged in Bill No. C-120 and which is to deal with railway rationalization will have authority to give consideration to all of these factors.
I do not want to disagree with the concern expressed by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) over railway abandonment. Nevertheless, it seems to me that setting a five year term between applications is to pass unduly rigid legislation prior to the passage of Bill No. C-120 at the next session of parliament, a bill which we hope will solve the whole problem. So while I agree with the concern that has been expressed, as I have said, I do not believe that Bill No. C-79 does handle the problem in the way which would be acceptable to the House of Commons and to Canadians generally, in face of the provisions of Bill No. C-120.

Mr. Speaker, the explanatory note of Bill No. C-79 stipulates:
The purpose of this bill is to provide that if the board of transport commissioners has refused an application made by a railway company for abandoning a line of railway-
Here, I make a digression. If a company decides to abandon a line, it is because that line is not profitable or its operation is no longer useful or profitable for the users thereof.
I continue to read the explanatory note.
-or has refused leave for removing, closing or abandoning any station or divisional point that would involve the removal of employees, no subsequent applications for such approval or for such leave could be entertained by the board during the next five years.
With regard to this explanatory note to Bill No. C-79, I understand that in the riding of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk), one may see such railway lines which are not profitable or which disappear precisely
Railway Act
because they are not adapted or are not-I would not say used-but conformable to the economic and social needs of our country.
The explanatory note continues:
The reason for the suggested amendments is that very often a railway company whose request has been turned down will renew its application from time to time, at short intervals, in the hope that the opposition has abated or will not be so active and consequently that the board will reverse its previous decision notwithstanding the fact that the situation is unchanged since the day of the original demand.
The new application is more in the nature of an appeal, from a refusal, to the same board.
That is the board of transport commissioners.
Neither I nor my group are opposed to all the citizens of the constituency of Marquette being treated equitably. Far from it, I will be the first to vote for any piece of legislation likely to help the citizens of Manitoba and more particularly those of the constituency of Marquette, since the bill is sponsored by the member for Marquette.
On the other hand, there is one point which we should greatly emphasize. Manitoba is not the only province in Canada; there are ten provinces, and in these ten provinces we have problems with the Department of Transport, in trying to minimize government interference in regard to transportation matters.
We think that the department or the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada is not being fair toward private enterprise or trucking operators, not only in the province of Quebec, but in all the other provinces.
With such a bill, it would be extremely difficult for the Canadian government to set up a dishonest or unfair commission or competition with regard to private enterprise.
